title: Definite vs Indefinite in the Past

sections.title: The same rule, one tense later
sections.content: Back in A1 you learned that Hungarian verbs conjugate differently depending on whether their object is definite (a/az, a specific known thing) or indefinite (egy, some, or no object at all) — kérek egy kávét next to kérem a kávét. That exact rule carries straight into the past tense: olvasott ("read something") next to olvasta ("read it"), the same egy/a-or-az test you already know how to apply.

sections.title: Indefinite and definite past, side by side

items.english: He/she read the book. (this particular book)
I ate up the soup. (this particular soup, all of it)

sections.content: meg- is one of the igekötők (verb prefixes) from Unit 22, but instead of showing direction it marks that an action is completely finished: megeszik means "to eat up, to finish eating" rather than just "to eat". Learn ettem/megettem as a pair for now — ettem just says you ate (something), while megettem says you finished it off.
